newsitem.title: UK: FUND VIEW-Guinness Flight goes for Chinese growth.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Guinness Flight goes for Chinese growth.

text.p: A new unit trust being launched this month by fund managers Guinness Flight aims to give retail investors exposure to China's burgeoning growth prospects via niche companies in Hong Kong and east Asia.
The Guinness Flight Asian Smaller Companies Trust aims to invest in about 70 listed Asian firms, each with a market capitalisation of between $50 million and $1.0 billion.
It says these smaller companies have greater growth potential than the region's traditional blue chips, due in part to the expansion of China's giant economy.
"China is certainly the engine for growth in the region," said Guinness Flight Director Philip Saunders. "There are varying degrees of impact but the most direct is obviously in Hong Kong."

The unit trust will have approximately five percent of its holdings in China, mostly through Hong Kong-listed shares, while the lion's share of the trust -- 45 percent -- will be invested in Hong Kong itself.
"Half of our Hong Kong exposure is to companies with important operations on the mainland," Saunders said, with most in manufacturing and services.
Many of the other companies in which the trust will invest elsewhere in the region will benefit at least indirectly from the expansion of the Chinese market, he added.
Official forecasts put GDP growth in China at 10 percent for 1997. Guinness Flight is expecting around 10.3 percent, while HSBC James Capel said last week it was going for 11 percent.

Some analysts say the Asian tigers -- Thailand, Taiwan, Singapore among others -- are maturing now and are unable to offer investors the 9.0 or 10 percent growth averaged in the decade up to the early 1990s.
But Nerissa Lee, who will manage the trust from Hong Kong, said the region still boasts great potential after careful stock selection.
Asian growth is still expected to average 6.0 to 8.0 percent in the medium term -- far above the 2.5 percent on average in western Europe or the United States.
And changes in the pattern of Asia's exports -- with intra-regional trade accounting now for 40 percent, at the expense of trade with the developed world -- should benefit these small cap firms.
"We believe that investment in Asia's smaller companies now represents one of the best ways to translate the region's superior growth rate into investment profits," Saunders said.
"Small to medium sized companies in the region generally have higher earnings growth and lower price earnings ratios than Asia's blue chips," he added.
The trust is designed as a sister to Guinness Flight's $22 million offshore Asia Small Companies Fund, which Lee also runs from Hong Kong together with the company's China fund.
Lee said the trust's overall sectoral bias lies in consumer-related manufacturing industries, adding she has bought shares in Thailand's Serm Suk and Hong Kong's Pacific Concord.
While many investors have bailed out of their investments in the ailing stock markets of Thailand and Indonesia, individual companies still present great opportunities, Lee said.

In addition to Hong Kong and China, 18 percent of the trust's assets will be invested in Malaysia, 13 percent in Singapore, 9.0 percent in Thailand, and 5.0 percent each in Indonesia and the Philippines.
While it has no exposure to Taiwan or South Korea, Lee said this may change if opportunities present themselves.
Saunders said the trust would like to see investments of around 10 billion stg when the fixed price offer period closes on November 12.
Minimum investment size is 1,000 stg, annual management fees are 1.5 percent, and the initial charge is 5.0 percent. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
